claim: Nematostella vectensis expresses toxins and stinging cells during early embryonic stages.
source: The appearance of toxins and stinging cells during early embryonic stages in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis suggests that venom is already expressed in eggs and larvae of this species.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Venom composition changes dramatically between developmental stages of Nematostella vectensis.
source: We find that venom composition and arsenal of toxin-producing cells change dramatically between developmental stages of this species.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic and proteomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different life stages of Nematostella have vastly different interspecific interactions.
source: These findings can be explained by the vastly different interspecific interactions of each life stage, as individuals develop from a miniature non-feeding mobile planula to a larger sessile polyp that predates on other animals and interact differently with predators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract, supported by behavioral assays described later in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral assays involving prey, predators and Nematostella are consistent with the hypothesis that venom composition changes are driven by different interspecific interactions.
source: Indeed, behavioral assays involving prey, predators and Nematostella are consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Animals with a complex life cycle have a wider and more dynamic venom landscape than initially appreciated.
source: Further, the results of this work suggest a much wider and dynamic venom landscape than initially appreciated in animals with a complex life cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Venoms and toxins are mostly used by animals for antagonistic interactions such as prey capture and defense from predators.
source: Venoms and the toxins they include are mostly used by animals for antagonistic interactions, such as prey capture and defense from predators (Fry et al., 2009; Casewell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological research on venoms has been focused almost exclusively on adult stages of animals.
source: Pharmacological research has been focused almost exclusively on the venoms of the adult stages despite the fact that many animals display remarkable transformations in body architectures and ecology during their development (Ruppert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as background information with a citation.

claim: Many animals display remarkable transformations in body architectures and ecology during their development.

claim: Vast differences in body architecture and ecology may dictate different interspecific interactions for distinct life stages.

source: During the Nematostella life cycle, females release a gelatinous egg package and males release sperm into the water (Hand and Uhlinger, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: After fertilization occurs in Nematostella, the zygote cleavage begins, forming a blastula.
source: After fertilization occurs, the zygote cleavage begins, forming a blastula and less than 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf) gastrulation is completed.
evidence: This is stated as a description of Nematostella development.

claim: Gastrulation is completed less than 24 hr post-fertilization in Nematostella.
source: After fertilization occurs, the zygote cleavage begins, forming a blastula and less than 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf) gastrulation is completed.
evidence: This is stated as a description of Nematostella development.

claim: A planula larva emerges from the egg package 48–72 hpf in Nematostella.
source: A planula larva emerges from the egg package 48–72 hpf and starts swimming in the water.
evidence: This is stated as a description of Nematostella development.

claim: Six to seven days after fertilization, the Nematostella planula settles in soft substrate and starts to metamorphose into a primary polyp.
source: Six to seven days after fertilization, the planula settles in soft substrate and starts to metamorphose into a primary polyp and sexual maturation takes about 4 months under lab conditions (Hand and Uhlinger, 1992) (Figure 1A).

claim: Sexual maturation in Nematostella takes about 4 months under lab conditions.
source: Six to seven days after fertilization, the planula settles in soft substrate and starts to metamorphose into a primary polyp and sexual maturation takes about 4 months under lab conditions (Hand and Uhlinger, 1992) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The Nematostella egg and planula are roughly spherical and measure only about 250 µm.
source: Whereas the egg and planula are roughly spherical and measure only about 250 µm, the morphologically differentiated elongated adult polyp can reach the length of 4 cm in the wild and up to 20 cm in the lab (Williams, 1975; Hand and Uhlinger, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The morphologically differentiated elongated adult Nematostella polyp can reach the length of 4 cm in the wild.
